title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the question of how artificial intelligence education can be made more accessible and relevant when embedded into existing K-12 subject areas. Rather than studying student learning outcomes, the authors focus on the design process itself and on teacher perspectives about integrating AI concepts into core curricula.

The study used a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 educators and educational directors. Participants first discussed AI concepts and tools, then worked in small groups with researchers to draft integrated lesson ideas for social studies, ESL, and literacy for students with learning disabilities. The workshop also included pre-work, presentations on AI and AI ethics, card sorting, and reflective discussions.

The main findings were that teachers valued curriculum supports for evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration, and that AI could be integrated into core subjects through data, reflection, and ethics. The literacy-related example was a curriculum for students with learning disabilities centered on vocabulary and image classification, but the paper does not evaluate learner outcomes or compare the AI curriculum against any control condition. The authors conclude that teacher co-design is important for making K-12 AI curriculum more accessible and implementable, especially outside computer science classrooms.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general artificial intelligence tool or system for K-12 AI education, including machine learning and AI learning tools used in classrooms rather than a specific commercial chatbot or named LLM product.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper did not evaluate a literacy AI tool in an instructional experiment. It described a co-design workshop where teachers designed an integrated literacy/AI curriculum concept using Google Teachable Machine and discussed other AI learning tools such as Machine Learning for Kids, Google Quick Draw, and MIT App Inventor.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative co-design/workshop paper rather than an experimental evaluation of a literacy AI tool. It provides design insights and proposed curricula, but no direct comparative outcome evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: No student outcome effects were measured, and there are no effect sizes or comparative literacy results reported. The paper does not provide evidence of instructional impact for a specific tool.
